content: Edema refers to the abnormal accumulation of fluid in the interstitial spaces of tissues. Edema can be a manifestation of systemic diseases such as nephrotic syndrome, right-sided heart failure, hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, adverse drug reactions, recent surgical complications, or malignancies. It may present as generalized edema, often associated with cardiac, thyroid, or renal disorders, or as localized edema, which can result from conditions like cellulitis, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), chronic venous insufficiency, or lymphedema. The diagnostic process involves a thorough history-taking, focusing on recent surgeries, trauma, systemic illnesses, or malignancies, as well as a physical examination to assess the distribution of edema and determine whether it is pitting or non-pitting. Pain elicited on palpation should also be evaluated. Duplex ultrasonography is a valuable tool for detecting evidence of DVT. In cases of localized edema with an unclear cause, further imaging studies such as abdominal computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance venography may be necessary. Life-Threatening Causes of Peripheral Edema Certain conditions causing peripheral edema can be life-threatening if not promptly treated. These include: Generalized edema resulting from decompensated heart failure. Localized leg edema caused by proximal DVT, which can lead to acute pulmonary embolism. Common Causes of Peripheral Edema Peripheral edema can also result from a variety of more common conditions, including: Advanced kidney disease. Nephrotic syndrome. Systolic or diastolic heart failure. Constrictive pericarditis. Pulmonary hypertension. Anemia. Nutritional deficiencies. Malabsorption syndromes. Refeeding edema. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Cellulitis. Superficial thrombophlebitis. Baker’s cyst. Chronic venous insufficiency. Lymphedema. Pregnancy. Menstrual cycle-related changes. Hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism. Medication side effects. Obstructive sleep apnea. Diagnostic Approach The diagnostic process for edema involves a structured algorithm that includes history-taking, physical examination, and appropriate imaging or laboratory studies to identify the underlying cause. Treatment Strategies The treatment of edema is guided by an algorithm that addresses the underlying cause and employs specific therapeutic interventions. Recommendations (Do’s) Before initiating medical compression therapy, assess arterial circulation. For proximal DVT, the use of compression bandages or medical compression stockings, combined with anticoagulant therapy and walking, can reduce pain and swelling. Compression therapy in DVT does not increase the risk of pulmonary thromboembolism or post-thrombotic syndrome. Early mobilization in acute DVT does not elevate the risk of pulmonary thromboembolism. In the acute phase of DVT, calf compression can help reduce irreversible skin changes, edema, and pain. In patients with compensated heart failure (NYHA Class I or II), mild compression of both legs may improve cardiac preload. Proper sizing of compression therapy is essential in diabetic neuropathy to prevent peripheral nerve damage, such as peroneal nerve palsy or foot drop. Obstructive sleep apnea in obese patients can cause bilateral leg edema due to pulmonary hypertension induced by hypoxia. After leg vein harvesting for bypass graft surgery, mild compression stockings (15-20 mmHg) significantly reduce leg edema. Daflon or micronized purified flavonoid fraction (MPFF) is recommended for chronic venous insufficiency due to its anti-inflammatory properties and ability to enhance venous contractility. Topical steroids may be beneficial for stasis dermatitis (characterized by scaling and erythematous skin changes) associated with chronic venous insufficiency or lymphedema. Contraindications (Don’ts) Avoid using medical compression devices in the following conditions: Severe peripheral arterial occlusive disease, defined by an ABI < 0. Suspected compression of bypassed arteries following coronary artery bypass graft surgery. Severe decompensated heart failure (NYHA Class IV), as increased preload can worsen right and left ventricular function. History of allergic reactions to compression materials. Severe diabetic neuropathy with sensory loss, microangiopathy, or risk of skin necrosis.
